pr_title: Avoid thundering herd of relists on etcd
pr_body:
Fix the problem of thundering herd of relists on etcd.

Fix: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/86483

When doing rolling upgrade of masters, with #83520 (already merged in 1.17):
- downing a single kube-apiserver results in breaking all the watches (particularly from kubelets and kube-proxies)
- terminating kube-apiserver doesn't trigger sending bookmarks to watches - they are currently send only right before timeout
- when watches are reconnecting to the newer apiserver, they often fail with "410 Gone" error
- that results in paginated relist with RV="", that is being served from etcd and is overloading control plane

With this PR, when watch returns "410 Gone":
- we fallback to List with RV="<rv of last observed object>"
- with the semantic of "at least as fresh as a given RV" that prevents going back in time
- only "410 Gone" from List results in fallback to RV="" paginates list

```release-note
Fix the masters rolling upgrade causing thundering herd of LISTs on etcd leading to control plane unavailability.
```

It occurred to me that a watch-cache enabled resource and a watch-cache disabled resource might behave in observably different ways on the initial list with resourceVersion=0&limit=500

The watch cache will ignore paging and return the full list of items. If there is no watch cache, does the etcd storage honor paging even at resourceVersion=0?

If so, would it make sense to use paged responses to the first resourceVersion=0 request as a hint to the client that 1) paging is honored, 2) watch cache is disabled for this resource, and 3) the resource is high cardinality enough to fill more than one page? That could help the client determine whether to page or not on subsequent requests for specific resourceVersions

> The watch cache will ignore paging and return the full list of items. If there is no watch cache, does the etcd storage honor paging even at resourceVersion=0?

Yes
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/blob/master/staging/src/k8s.io/apiserver/pkg/storage/etcd3/store.go#L552

> If so, would it make sense to use paged responses to the first resourceVersion=0 request as a hint to the client that 1) paging is honored, 2) watch cache is disabled for this resource, and 3) the resource is high cardinality enough to fill more than one page? That could help the client determine whether to page or not on subsequent requests for specific resourceVersions

I'm not sure.
That works only assuming that at start of reflector there are already enough objects of a given type to return. For short-living clusters (and with batch workloads we're seeing more and more of these), when those start the cluster is empty, so we may not be able to detect anything. Whereas later listing from watchcache may be necessary.
My main concern is that the only signal to use is whether more than one page was returned. 

I think that what I'm proposing is more error-prone (though I definitely agree it's also not fully robust).

FTR from our offline conversation:

Jordan: I agree it doesn't catch all scenarios, but would cover the one I care about most which is upgrades of existing large clusters
me: the question is whether it won't break "creating new large clusters" - this is what I'm concerned about mostly

I think basing the client approach on observed server capabilities is better than waiting until we've already caused load/timeout errors on the server, and then trying to distinguish between network errors and timeouts due to this problem and due to other issues.

> I think basing the client approach on observed server capabilities is better than waiting until we've already caused load/timeout errors on the server, and then trying to distinguish between network errors and timeouts due to this problem and due to other issues.

Thinking more about this, I actually realized that with this approach we will be erroring on the side of listing from cache.
As an example, for the empty cluster, say LIST pods may fit one page (which will trigger switching off pagination), even though it may not be the case later.

So assuming the behavior will be:
- default to list from cache (when RV!="" && RV!="0")
- if the initial list (the one from start with RV="0") was paginated, then actually force pagination later too
then that sounds safe from scalability POV.

@liggitt - is that acceptable for you? If so, I will rework the second commit when I find some time (though I'm OOO until end of next week).
That's the safest approach I could think of that seemed straightforward to implement. Unless someone has a better idea, I think we should proceed with that.

issue_context.title: 1.17 & 1.18 clusters are failing during master rolling upgrade
issue_context.body:
https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/83520 changed the way how reflectors work.
In particular, when we down kube-apiserver, what happens is:
- watches (from kubelets/kube-proxies) are breaking and reconnecting to a different apiserver
- apiserver (when restarting) initializes watch cache at "now"
- given that bookmarks (in the current implementation) are send only right before watch is timing out, when we down kube-apiserver, they are not send

So in large cluster, when we down the last kube-apiserver, in many cases the watches are reconnecting to new enough apiserver and are failing with "error too old".
As a result, with https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/83520, we move the mode for relisting from etcd, and that kills apiserver
(mostly because when kubelet lists pods from its node, from cache we send only those, but from etcd we need to list everything, deserialize and filtter out).


Two main ideas how we can mitigate it is:
- change the reflector to instead try to list from cache - some approach can be find here: https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/86430
- send bookmarks more frequently (though we didn't validate the performance impact and that won't help in all cases)
- improve throttling of LIST requests (but the problem is that with pagination, we risk of not making any progress if continuations will be rejected and then failing with "out-of-window" errors)

I think the most promising and minimal change (given that we should cherrypick that to 1.17) seems to be some variation of (1), but we need more time to evaluate it properly.

@kubernetes/sig-scalability-bugs 
@kubernetes/sig-api-machinery-bugs 
@smarterclayton @liggitt @jpbetz @mm4tt
comments: We will provide more exact data once we have concrete numbers and comparisons.

my immediate inclination would be to revert the client-side bits of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/83520 for 1.17.1 until we have more data and tests in place, rather than leave it as-is or experiment in patch releases.

> change the reflector to instead try to list from cache - some approach can be find here: #86430

isn't dropping the limit on reflector relist likely to crush servers running without the watch cache enabled? @smarterclayton might have better data on what that looks like.

Option #2
```
send bookmarks more frequently
```
Can we send the bookmark right before shutting down api-server (not increasing frequency of sending bookmarks) ?

> Can we send the bookmark right before shutting down api-server (not increasing frequency of sending bookmarks) ?

That doesn't work if e.g. machine is hard-rebooted or sth, so I wouldn't treat is as very full solution.


>> change the reflector to instead try to list from cache - some approach can be find here: #86430

> isn't dropping the limit on reflector relist likely to crush servers running without the watch cache enabled? @smarterclayton might have better data on what that looks like.

@liggitt - that is good question. But my claim is that you can't have very large clusters withou watch cache enabled (at least for couple main high-volume resources like endpoints, nodes and pods). So I'm personally not too worried about that.

I ran the following experiment to confirm that this is an actual regression between `1.16` and `1.17`

## Experiment

1. Set up two 5K node clusters (`VERSION=1.16.4` and `VERSION=1.17.0`)
```
kubetest --up \
  --extract=gs://kubernetes-release/release/$VERSION \
  --gcp-nodes=5000 \
  --gcp-project=$PROJECT \
  --gcp-zone=$ZONE \
  --provider=gce
```

2. Wait for cluster to go up, set up prometheus monitoring using `ClusterLoader2`

3. Reboot master VM
    1. `gcloud compute instances stop --project=$PROJECT --zone=$ZONE $MASTER_NAME`
    1. `sleep 2m`
    1. `gcloud compute instances start --project=$PROJECT --zone=$ZONE $MASTER_NAME`
    1. `sleep 2m && sudo ip route del to local 10.40.0.2/32 dev eth0` (needed due to https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/issues/86547)

4. Observe...

## Results

### **1.16.4**

1. It took ~2 min since the master VM (and network to it) went up till the cluster *stabilized*. By *stabilized* I mean that the traffic pattern and the Scalability SLIs (e.g. api-call-latency) went back to what they were before the restart.
2. Some graphs (with comments)
    ![O5ep5phwiLP (1)](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2604887/71368664-cbabf880-25a8-11ea-81c5-b5bda1cdfbc6.png)
    ![L0TkdrMSWqd](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2604887/71573757-b887b400-2ae5-11ea-8144-5c92811ec316.png)


3. Overall, this looks really good

### **1.17.0**

1. Master never stabilized after restart, api-server went into crash loop
2. Some graphs with comments, confirming that this is kind of a *thundering herd* issue. After master reboots, **etcd gets hit with 100-200 QPS of LIST requests per resource for multiple resources (SIC!)** which in turn overloads the system. Once this happens we run into the known *vicious circle* problem: system is overloaded -> we hit inflight-requests limits -> some important requests get dropped (e.g. leader election) -> more components restart and issue list request to initialize local cache -> system gets even more overloaded -> ...
    ![okFUcZVcsVk](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2604887/71369278-88eb2000-25aa-11ea-9a04-61b89da555bf.png)
    ![shewEYoUzy6](https://user-images.githubusercontent.com/2604887/71369333-b46e0a80-25aa-11ea-86f7-af331a4d0d95.png)


In general, this is really bad. We have to fix it (or revert the https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/83520) in 1.17.1

@wojtek-t for future reference, the best way to contact the CI signal team is @kubernetes/ci-signal :) We introduced it this iteration, I think it's not that well-known yet.

And thanks for filing this!

The current version of https://github.com/kubernetes/kubernetes/pull/86430 seem to mitigate the problems that we found internally.
@mm4tt will run his tests (that he described above) to (hopefully) prove that it helps in this case too.

I ran the tests and can confirm that the fix helps. 
Master stabilized, there was no significant increase in the number of etcd list requests after the restart. 

If someone would like to take a look at the graphs, they can be found at http://35.237.122.182:3000/d/UkaNrXBZk/master-down-up-experiment?orgId=1&var-source=master-down-up-5k-k8s-1-18-fix&from=1577717822588&to=1577721055853

> send bookmarks more frequently

Because the watcher will rewatch in 5-10 minutes, we find in practice that it is more appropriate to send a bookmark in 1-2 minutes if no event has been sent.

> change the reflector to instead try to list from cache 

This works well on most cases, and the final bottleneck will become apiserver memory limit. Because apiserver cache does not support page list, list from apiserver cache consumes apiserver memory. There are two solutions to this problem. One is to add an interface to apiserver, which sends list data in a stream similar to watch, and the other is to extend the apiserver to support the page list, but the apiserver does not have multiple versions of data and we can limit the page list support to a single server.

#86824 fixes the issue for 1.17, will be releases in 1.17.1

#86430 will resolve this for 1.18
